newsitem.title: USA: Anaheim, Calif., council okays Walt Disney expansion.
newsitem.headline: Anaheim, Calif., council okays Walt Disney expansion.

text.p: Elected officials in Anaheim, Calif., late on Tuesday approved Walt Disney Co.'s $1.4 billion expansion of its Disneyland resort.
At a meeting in Anaheim that stretched into the night, the city council voted 5-0 in favor of the development plan for the project, Anaheim spokesman Bret Colson said.

The city council also approved a financial agreement that would provide $546 million for infrastructure improvements to the area around the proposed theme park and for the city's convention facilities. To help fund these improvements, the city plans to issue revenue bonds, backed in part by Disney, city officials said.
Disney officials estimated that the massive project would create 14,500 new jobs in southern California, including 8,100 in Anaheim.
Anaheim officials said the project would bolster city revenues because the expanded facilities would draw more visitors, larger convention groups and increase hotel occupancy.
Anaheim Mayor Tom Daly said the agreement would secure the "city's economic future."

Disney said it intends to build the theme park, called "Disney's California Adventure," next to its famed Disneyland complex. Construction of the second theme park was expected to begin in early 1997 with completion planned by the year 2001.

The first-phase expansion plans would include 750 new hotel rooms within a deluxe resort hotel and the Disneyland Center, a retail, dining and entertainment center that will cater to guests and convention visitors.
As part of the deal, the city agreed that $546 million would be spent on improvements to surrounding areas, including a $150 million expansion of the city's convention center.

To help raise funds for these improvements, the city was expected to issue $395 million of revenue bonds. Officials said that state and federal grants as well as hotel and bed tax revenues would back the $546 million of proposed improvements. Disney would provide some credit support for the bonds to help protect the city's budget.

"This project is the best, most cost-effective way to deliver the necessary enhancements to the tourism district surrounding Disneyland," Daly said. "We believe the expansion will increase tourism and help avoid stagnation."

Despite the city council vote, Colson said the plan would face some hurdles. A local tax measure on the Nov. 5 ballot is a critical funding element of the infrastructure agreement. Colson said the city does not plan to issue the bonds for the improvements before the November vote.
